label: Chapter 4
title: Beyond the blog
dek: Release by release, “blog” stopped being a big enough word for what people were building.

blocks.text: Pages had arrived in 2005 under a modest heading: “Manage More Than Your Blog.”[^wp15] Two years later, version 2.1 let any page stand as a site’s front door, “making it much easier to use WordPress as a content management system.”[^wp21]

blocks: A content management system, or CMS, runs a whole website: standing pages, menus, people with different permissions, kinds of content its authors never imagined. WordPress acquired these in pieces — user roles in 2.0, widgets in 2.2, tags in 2.3, a history of revisions in 2.6.[^wp20][^wp22][^wp23][^wp26]

The pieces also had to be usable. For 2.7, in 2008, a redesigned admin was tested by outside researchers first. Every participant preferred the rough prototype, codenamed Crazyhorse, to what they had — “and it wasn’t even pretty,” Jane Wells reported.[^crazyhorse]

WordPress 3.0, on 17 June 2010, gathered it up. Custom post types let a site hold things that were neither posts nor pages: products, events, recipes. Menus, adapted from a navigation system the core team asked the theme company WooThemes to contribute, could be arranged without editing a file.[^menus] A separate edition for running many sites at once was folded in, so one installation could serve “one blog or ten million.”[^wp30]

blocks.name: beyond
blocks.caption: Kiln Diary around 2010, in a reconstruction of the Twenty Ten theme: a menu across the top, and a set of “pots” that are their own kind of content. Beside it, three invented sites of kinds that had become ordinary.

blocks: By then the British Prime Minister’s office was reported to have relaunched its site on WordPress, and one American university ran more than three thousand blogs for students and staff on a single installation.[^number10][^umw] Their keepers had new things to think about: updates, permissions, plugins that disagreed with one another.

blocks.label: A correction worth making
blocks.text: Custom post types are often dated to 3.0. An interface for them was already in 2.9, and custom taxonomies in 2.5; version 3.0 is where they became practical.[^wp29][^wp25]

blocks.title: From blog to CMS, release by release

rows: User roles; a visual editor; Akismet bundled.[^wp20]
A page can be the front page.[^wp21]
Tags and a new taxonomy system; update notifications.[^wp23]
A redesign with the studio Happy Cog; galleries and shortcodes.[^wp25]
The Crazyhorse admin; one-click upgrades; a plugin installer.[^wp27]
Trash, an image editor, post thumbnails.[^wp29]
Menus, post types, Multisite, and Twenty Ten — the first new default theme since Kubrick. 218 people credited.[^wp30]
A re-imagined flow for uploading media and building galleries.[^wp35]

items.text: This is a landmark for us, as it is the first time we’ve won this award, and it marks a shift in the public perception of WordPress, from blog software to full-featured CMS.
items.where: on winning an open-source CMS award

items.text: By late 2006 three people could commit code: Matt Mullenweg, Ryan Boren and, newly, Mark Jaquith.[^wp205] By the 3.0 announcement the list of committers had twelve names.[^wp30] In January 2010 Mullenweg wrote that commit access should become “more a recognition of trust, quality, and most importantly activity,” separate from the title of lead developer.[^dd32]
After 3.0 the team paused: “We’re going to take a release cycle off to focus on all of the things around WordPress.”[^wp30]
